title: Public Key Cryptography
body:
**Two keys instead of one.** A public key $e$ that anybody may have, and a private key $d$ that
only the owner holds, with the property that

$$D_d(E_e(m)) = m$$

and knowing $e$ does not let you compute $d$. Anyone can encrypt to you; only you can decrypt.

Diffie and Hellman published the idea in 1976 and it is the single largest conceptual jump in the
subject, because it solves the problem [[Symmetric Key Cryptography|symmetric cryptography]] cannot
touch: **two strangers who have never met can agree on a secret over a channel the adversary is
listening to.** Before 1976 that was believed impossible.

## What makes it possible

A **one-way function with a trapdoor**: easy to compute, hard to invert, unless you hold a piece of
extra information.

| Scheme | Easy | Hard without the trapdoor | Trapdoor |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[RSA]] | multiply two primes | factor the product | the primes $p, q$ |
| [[Diffie-Hellman]], [[ElGamal]] | modular exponentiation $g^x$ | recover $x$ ([[Discrete Logarithm Problem]]) | the exponent |
| [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] | scalar multiply a point | recover the scalar (ECDLP) | the scalar |

Every entry rests on a **hardness assumption**, not a theorem. Nobody has proved factoring is hard;
if someone finds a polynomial factoring algorithm, RSA ends that day. This is the honest difference
between public-key cryptography and the one-time pad, whose security is proved outright, and
between it and [[NP-Complete|NP-hardness]], which is worst-case and therefore the wrong shape:
cryptography needs a *random* instance to be hard, which is a strictly stronger requirement.

## The algebra is the whole subject

Every scheme in this block is a statement about a finite [[Group]]:

- [[RSA]] works in $\mathbb{Z}_n^*$, the invertible elements mod $n = pq$, whose order is
  $\phi(n)$. Decryption works because $a^{\phi(n)} \equiv 1$, which is Euler's theorem, which is a
  corollary of [[Lagrange's Theorem]].
- Diffie-Hellman and [[ElGamal]] work in a [[Cyclic Group]] of large prime order, usually a
  subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$. The security parameter is the *order of the group*, and the
  operation is [[Modular Arithmetic|modular exponentiation]].
- [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] changes only the group, keeping every protocol identical.

That last point is the one worth carrying: **the protocols are group-theoretic and the group is a
parameter.** Diffie-Hellman written abstractly does not mention primes at all, and swapping in the
elliptic curve group is what shrinks the key from 3072 bits to 256.

## What it costs, and hybrid encryption

Public-key operations are modular exponentiations on 2048-bit numbers, roughly a thousand times
slower per byte than [[AES]]. **So nobody encrypts data with it.** Every real system is hybrid:

```
1. public-key handshake agrees a random 256-bit session key
2. AES-GCM encrypts the actual traffic with that key
3. session key is discarded when the connection closes
```

That is what a TLS handshake is. Public-key cryptography's job is **key transport and
authentication**, and step 2 is where the bytes go. It also gives *forward secrecy* when the
handshake is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman: compromising the long-term private key later does not
decrypt recorded past sessions, because the session key was never transmitted.

## The problem it does not solve

**Authenticity of the public key itself.** If an attacker can substitute their own public key for
Bob's, they read everything: the man-in-the-middle attack, and it defeats plain Diffie-Hellman
completely. The mathematics cannot fix this, because both keys are equally valid mathematically.
The answer is [[Digital Signature|signatures]] and a trust hierarchy: a certificate authority signs
"this key belongs to Bob", your browser ships with the CA's key, and the problem is reduced rather
than eliminated. See [[HTTPS]] for the deployment.
